results.author: coygeek opened on
results.text:
fix(docs): packaged migration README links resolve outside the installed packages · Issue #2734 · supabase/supabase-js · GitHub

 #2734

## Description

coygeek

on Oct 3, 2026

## Summary

The `migrations/README.md` shipped by all six core `@supabase/*` packages at `2.117.2` links cross-cutting migration guidance to `../../../../docs/MIGRATION.md`. This relative path works in the source monorepo, but in a normal `node_modules/@supabase/ /migrations/` layout it resolves to the consuming application's `docs/MIGRATION.md`. That file is absent in a fresh application and is not included in any of the six package tarballs.

## Steps to reproduce

Download the published artifacts without running package scripts, expand them into their normal installed layout, and resolve the shipped links:

```
repro_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
cd "$repro_dir"
npm pack --ignore-scripts --silent \
  @supabase/[email protected] @supabase/[email protected] \
  @supabase/[email protected] @supabase/[email protected] \
  @supabase/[email protected] @supabase/[email protected]
for name in supabase-js auth-js functions-js postgrest-js realtime-js storage-js; do
  mkdir -p "node_modules/@supabase/$name"
  tar -xzf "supabase-$name-2.117.2.tgz" \
    -C "node_modules/@supabase/$name" --strip-components=1
done
node <<'JS'
const fs = require('node:fs');
const path = require('node:path');
for (const name of ['supabase-js', 'auth-js', 'functions-js', 'postgrest-js', 'realtime-js', 'storage-js']) {
  const file = `node_modules/@supabase/${name}/migrations/README.md`;
  const text = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
  const relative = text.match(/\]\(([^)]+docs\/MIGRATION\.md)\)/)?.[1];
  if (!relative) throw new Error(`No cross-cutting migration link in ${file}`);
  const target = path.normalize(path.join(path.dirname(file), relative));
  console.log(`${name}: ${relative} -> ${target}; exists=${fs.existsSync(target)}`);
}
JS
```

## Expected behavior

A developer or agent following cross-cutting migration guidance from a published package reaches the SDK's migration document. The target should remain valid outside a source checkout and identify the applicable SDK version.

## Actual behavior

Each package produces the same unresolved target:

```
supabase-js: ../../../../docs/MIGRATION.md -> docs/MIGRATION.md; exists=false
auth-js: ../../../../docs/MIGRATION.md -> docs/MIGRATION.md; exists=false
functions-js: ../../../../docs/MIGRATION.md -> docs/MIGRATION.md; exists=false
postgrest-js: ../../../../docs/MIGRATION.md -> docs/MIGRATION.md; exists=false
realtime-js: ../../../../docs/MIGRATION.md -> docs/MIGRATION.md; exists=false
storage-js: ../../../../docs/MIGRATION.md -> docs/MIGRATION.md; exists=false

```

The package-local `AGENTS.md` routes users to this migration directory, whose README explicitly describes the notes as shipped and version-pinned. Its cross-cutting link instead depends on the source repository's directory layout.

## Affected area

`packages/core/{auth-js,functions-js,postgrest-js,realtime-js,storage-js,supabase-js}/migrations/README.md` and their published npm counterparts. This report concerns the packaged link; the same relative link resolves correctly inside the source monorepo.

## Runtime or environment

All six npm packages were verified at `2.117.2`, which remains the registry's `latest` stable version. The reproduction ran with Node.js `22.23.2` and npm `12.0.2`. It needs no Supabase service, database, credentials, or SDK import.

## Evidence

- The supabase-js migration README at current master contains the relative link. All six corresponding source READMEs are byte-identical to the READMEs in their published `2.117.2` tarballs. The downloaded tarballs matched the npm registry's SHA512 integrity values.
- PR #2397 established the package-local agent entry points and shipped migration notes. Its intended installed-package workflow makes this link relevant to package consumers.
- I reviewed all five commits from stable `v2.117.2` at `6d21e3fc8cd

results.title: Supabase Client Setup: Publishable and Secret API Keys — Urhoba
results.author: Ahmet Bohur
results.text:
Supabase Client Setup: Publishable and Secret API Keys — Urhoba

2026-09-27· 9 min read

# Supabase Client Setup and API Keys

Configure supabase-js 2.117 with the right key in the right place: publishable keys for browsers and apps, secret keys only on servers, what the legacy anon and service_role keys become, and why a client-safe key protects nothing without access policies.

Contents

We now have a schema with migrations and generated types (chapter 4). Next, the application needs to talk to Supabase. That takes a project URL, an API key and a client instance. The code is short. The decisions around it are where security incidents come from: which key goes into the browser bundle, which stays on the server, and what each key actually allows.

## Prerequisites and assumptions#

- `@supabase/supabase-js` 2.117.2 (npm `latest`, 27 September 2026). Version 3 is only on the `next` tag, so don't use it for production.
- TypeScript, with the `Database` type generated in chapter 4.
- What I ran: I type-checked every client file below with TypeScript 7.0.2 in strict mode. I ran the queries against a local PostgREST 16.3 and Supabase Auth v2.197.0 on PostgreSQL 16. In front of them I put a small stand-in for the Supabase gateway that maps keys to roles the way the API-keys page describes. The hosted gateway's own behaviour, such as rejecting secret keys from browsers, is quoted from the docs, not tested.

## The four key types#

Supabase's API-keys page currently describes four keys:

| Key | Format | Postgres role | Where it belongs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Publishable | `sb_publishable_...` | `anon`, or `authenticated` when a user token is attached | Browsers, mobile and desktop apps, CLIs, public repos |
| Secret | `sb_secret_...` | `service_role` (bypasses RLS) | Servers, Edge Functions, jobs, anything you fully control |
| Legacy `anon` | Long-lived JWT | `anon` / `authenticated` | Same as publishable; being phased out |
| Legacy `service_role` | Long-lived JWT | `service_role` | Same as secret; being phased out |

A few details from the docs matter in practice:

- The new keys are not JWTs. "Publishable and secret keys are short strings, not JWTs." They go in the `apikey` header, not in `Authorization: Bearer`. supabase-js handles this for you. Hand-written `fetch` calls and old middleware that try to verify the key as a JWT will fail.
- The legacy keys are being retired. Supabase is "deprecating the `anon` and `service_role` keys by the end of 2026." New projects and new code should use publishable and secret keys.
- Secret keys refuse to work from browsers. The docs say Supabase matches on the `User-Agent` header and returns `401 Unauthorized`. Treat that as a safety net, not a design: a leaked key still works from `curl`.
- You can have several secret keys. The recommendation is one per backend component, "If one component leaks its key, you only rotate that one."

User sessions are separate from API keys. When a user signs in, Auth issues an access token, a JWT signed with the project's signing keys, and the client sends it as `Authorization: Bearer `. The API key says which project and which baseline role. The access token says which user.

## What a publishable key does and does not protect#

This is the idea to hold on to: everything the `anon` and `authenticated` roles are allowed to do, anyone on the internet can do. The publishable key is in your JavaScript bundle and your mobile app binary, and extracting it takes seconds. Sign-up is usually open, so becoming `authenticated` is just as easy.

A client-safe key is therefore only as safe as your grants and RLS policies. With the chapter 3 migration, RLS is on and no grants exist yet. In my local setup, an anonymous request to `profiles` with only a publishable key returned:

Copy

```
status 401, code 42501 — permission denied for table profiles
```

That is the correct result. Chapters 9 and 10 grant access row by row. If you disabled RLS "just to get started",

# Supabase Changelog

## An outdated subset of TLS 1.2 ciphers will be disabled on project HTTP APIs

2026-10-12 · Breaking Change · Auth, Data APIs, Storage, Realtime, Edge Functions · supabase.com/changelog/cbc-tls-ciphers-deprecated

Supabase will be disabling a subset of TLS 1.2 ciphers on project HTTP APIs on November 10, 2026. Clients that don't support modern standards (<0.0001% of Supabase traffic) will fail to connect.

---

## ASP.NET Core dependency injection for the Supabase .NET SDK

2026-10-12 · New Feature · supabase-dotnet · supabase.com/changelog/dotnet-dependency-injection-extension

The .NET SDK now ships an ASP.NET Core dependency injection package. A single method registers the main client and all sub-clients, so you don't have to wire it up by hand.

---

## The Supabase .NET SDK is now officially supported

2026-10-09 · New Feature · supabase-dotnet · supabase.com/changelog/supabase-dotnet-official-support

The .NET SDK for Supabase is now officially supported. It's the recommended way to build on Supabase from any .NET platform: ASP.NET, Blazor, MAUI, Unity, Azure, and more.

---

## Status page moves to incident.io

2026-10-08 · Improvement · Website · supabase.com/changelog/status-page-migration

status.supabase.com now runs on incident.io. Email subscribers carry over. SMS, Slack, webhook, and RSS subscribers must resubscribe; the new page supports only Email, RSS, and Slack.

---

## Scoped personal access tokens are now generally available

2026-10-06 · New Feature · Platform, Security, CLI, AI · supabase.com/changelog/scoped-personal-access-tokens-ga

Scoped personal access tokens are now available to everyone. Limit a token to specific projects or organizations and grant only the permissions it needs on the Management API, MCP server, and CLI.

---

## Organization invites support the No access role

2026-10-05 · Improvement · Platform, Studio, Security · supabase.com/changelog/no-access-org-role

Organization invites on Team and Enterprise plans now support the No access role, so admins can default new members to zero project access instead of Read-only access to every project.

---

## Framework adapters in @supabase/server are deprecated

2026-10-05 · Deprecation · supabase-server · supabase.com/changelog/supabase-server-adapters-deprecated

The Hono, H3, Elysia, and NestJS adapters in @supabase/server are deprecated and will be removed on December 1, 2026. Move to the framework bridges in the frameworks guide.

---

## [Private Alpha] Multigres: operating system for Postgres

2026-10-01 · New Feature · Database, Multigres · supabase.com/changelog/multigres-private-alpha

Run Supabase with multi-AZ high availability (HA), automatic failover, and scalable connection pooling. Multigres is now in Private Alpha for selected Pro, Team, and Enterprise organizations.

---

## OrioleDB is now in Public Beta with paid plans and paid features

2026-10-01 · Policy · Database, Studio, CLI, Auth, Storage, Realtime, Edge Functions · supabase.com/changelog/orioledb-public-beta

OrioleDB is now in Public Beta. Create OrioleDB projects on Free, Pro, Team, and Enterprise plans, with paid features and standard Postgres pricing. Existing alpha projects don't change.

---

## Supabase Middleware 1.0

2026-09-30 · New Feature · Edge Functions, supabase-js, supabase-middleware, supabase-server · supabase.com/changelog/supabase-middleware-1-0

@supabase/middleware 1.0.0 is stable: typed, composable middleware for fetch handlers. The engine runs wherever fetch runs, standalone or inside a framework through a short bridge you copy.

---

## PostgreSQL 15.19 / 17.11 minor release — action may be required for ltree, pgcrypto, btree_gist, and custom operators

2026-09-25 · Breaking Change · Database · supabase.com/changelog/postgres-15-19-17-11-breaking-changes

Postgres minor upgrade to 15.19/17.11 fixes 44 CVEs.
ltree and btree_gist indexes may need reindexing, and pgcrypto data encrypted with legacy ciphers needs re-en

results.title: Supabase error 42501: new row violates row-level security policy
results.text:
Supabase error 42501: new row violates row-level security policy

Entry No.047· Database· Oct 7, 2026· 6 min read

# Supabase error 42501: new row violates row-level security policy

Supabase's 42501 has two messages and seven causes. Each reproduced on a local stack, plus the October 30 change that breaks new tables.

The error, verbatim

```
{
  code: '42501',
  details: null,
  hint: null,
  message: 'new row violates row-level security policy for table "profiles"'
}

```

Tested on

supabase-js

2.117.2

Supabase CLI

2.120.0 (local stack)

Postgres

17.11

PostgREST

16.4

Node / OS

24.14.0 / Windows 11 Pro

Contents

1. Which policy is missing 01
2. .insert().select() needs a SELECT policy too 02
3. You’re not signed in (yet) 03
4. user_id isn’t sent, so the check fails 04
5. Upsert: the “(USING expression)” version 05
6. Storage uploads 06
7. “permission denied for table”: the October 30 change 07
8. What didn’t work 08
9. How this was tested 09

`42501` is Postgres’s code for “insufficient privilege”. Supabase returns it in two very different situations, and the message tells you which one you’re in:

| Message | What blocked the request | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `new row violates row-level security policy for table "x"` | A row-level security (RLS) policy | `401` signed out, `403` signed in |
| `new row violates row-level security policy (USING expression) for table "x"` | The same, on an upsert that hit an existing row | `403` |
| `new row violates row-level security policy` (no table name) | A Storage upload | `statusCode: "403"` |
| `permission denied for table x` | A missing table GRANT (not a policy) | `401` / `403` |

The first three are about policies. The last one is about grants, and it’s the one that will suddenly show up on existing projects after October 30, 2026 (see the last section). Adding a policy does nothing for it, and I tested that.

I reproduced every row of that table on a local Supabase stack, with `supabase-js` calling the real API. Each section below starts with what triggered it and ends with the change that made the same call succeed.

## Which policy is missing

Supabase’s RLS denies by default, per operation. A table with RLS on and only a SELECT policy can be read but not written. Inserting with the publishable (anon) key returned:

```
status: 401 Unauthorized
code: '42501'
message: 'new row violates row-level security policy for table "notes_selectonly"'
```

The same table with no policies at all behaved differently for reads: `select()` came back `200` with `data: []`. No error, just an empty list. So “reads work, writes fail” usually means you wrote a read policy and nothing else.

Add a policy for the operation that failed. For a table anyone can write to:

```
create policy "anyone can insert" on public.notes_selectonly
  for insert to anon, authenticated
  with check (true);
```

For rows that belong to a user (the usual `profiles` case), check the owner:

```
create policy "insert own profile" on public.profiles
  for insert to authenticated
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = id);
```

✓ Worked

With the policy in place, the same insert returned `201 Created`.

## `.insert().select()` needs a SELECT policy too

This one catches people who did write an INSERT policy. With only an INSERT policy on the table:

- `insert({ body: 'x' })` returned `201 Created`.
- `insert({ body: 'x' }).select()` returned `401` and the same 42501 message.

Asking for the row back means Postgres has to be allowed to read the new row, and without a SELECT policy it isn’t. The whole insert is rolled back: I counted the rows afterwards, and the failed call left nothing behind.

Add a SELECT policy that covers the new row:

```
create policy "anyone can read" on public.notes_insertonly
  for select to anon, authenticated
  using (true);
```

✓ Worked

`insert().select()` then returned `201` with the new row in `data`.

## You’re not signed in (yet)

A policy written `to authenticated` doesn’t appl

results.title: Supabase Auth: Sign-Up, Login and Session Handling — Urhoba
results.author: Ahmet Bohur
results.text:
Supabase Auth: Sign-Up, Login and Session Handling — Urhoba

2026-09-27· 11 min read

# Supabase Auth: Signup, Login and Sessions

Implement email and password sign-up, confirmation, login, logout and session tracking with supabase-js, handle each error state by code, and keep authentication (who you are) separate from authorization and account-confirmation policy.

Contents

Every query in chapter 6 assumed a signed-in user. This chapter provides one. We implement email-and-password sign-up with confirmation, login, logout and session tracking for the task board, and we handle every failure path deliberately. Along the way we separate three ideas that are easy to blur:

- Authentication answers who is making this request? Supabase Auth does this and proves it with a signed access token.
- Account policy answers which accounts may sign in at all? Examples: must the email be confirmed, are sign-ups open. These are Auth settings.
- Authorization answers what may this user do with this board? Your RLS policies decide this in the database (chapters 9–10), never Auth and never the UI.

A confirmed email proves the user controls an inbox. It says nothing about which boards they may edit.

## Prerequisites and assumptions#

- `@supabase/supabase-js` 2.117.2 and the client from chapter 5.
- The `handle_new_user()` trigger from chapter 3, which creates a `profiles` row for each new user.
- An app callback URL, `http://localhost:5173/auth/callback`, that is on the redirect allowlist (chapter 2's `config.toml`, and the dashboard for hosted projects).
- What I ran: the code below, type-checked with TypeScript 7.0.2, against the Supabase Auth server v2.197.0 (the release the CLI 2.118.0 stack uses) and PostgREST 16.3 on PostgreSQL 16. Email confirmation was on and emails went to a local SMTP sink. The run's output is quoted below. A hosted project adds its own gateway, email provider and rate limits.

## Confirmation: a policy you must choose#

The password guide says hosted projects require email confirmation by default, while local and self-hosted setups default to it being off. The local `config.toml` has `enable_confirmations = false`. That difference changes what `signUp` returns:

- Confirmation off:`signUp` returns a user and a session. The user is signed in immediately.
- Confirmation on:`signUp` returns a user and `session: null`. An email with a confirmation link is sent. Signing in before confirming fails.

Turn confirmation on locally so you develop against the production behaviour:

toml Copy

```
# supabase/config.toml
[auth.email]
enable_confirmations = true
```

Locally, the CLI stack captures outgoing mail in a web inbox (Mailpit), so you can click the links.

## The auth module#

ts Copy

```
// src/auth.ts — auth helpers for the task board
import type { AuthError } from '@supabase/supabase-js'
import { supabase } from './supabase'
 
const AUTH_CALLBACK_URL = process.env.AUTH_CALLBACK_URL ?? 'http://localhost:5173/auth/callback'
 
export type AuthResult =
  | { kind: 'signed-in'; userId: string }
  | { kind: 'check-email'; email: string }
  | { kind: 'error'; message: string; code?: string }
 
function describe(error: AuthError): AuthResult {
  switch (error.code) {
    case 'invalid_credentials':
      return { kind: 'error', code: error.code, message: 'Email or password is incorrect.' }
    case 'email_not_confirmed':
      return { kind: 'error', code: error.code, message: 'Confirm your email address first.' }
    case 'weak_password':
      return { kind: 'error', code: error.code, message: 'Choose a longer password.' }
    case 'over_request_rate_limit':
    case 'over_email_send_rate_limit':
      return { kind: 'error', code: error.code, message: 'Too many attempts. Try again later.' }
  }
  return { kind: 'error', code: error.code, message: 'Something went wrong. Please try again.' }
}
